summary: Global Burn Log is a free web app that turns 25 years of NASA satellite fire detections into a burning-activity calendar for any place on Earth. The record is split across sensors that cannot be compared directly: VIIRS (375 m) finds far more small fires than MODIS (1 km), so raw counts for India jump about 6.5 times in 2012. We count burning cell-days on a hexagon grid, make VIIRS MODIS-equivalent, and learn seasonal ratios between MODIS Terra, MODIS Aqua and VIIRS, with an uncertainty band on every estimated day. After harmonising, the jump is gone. Users pick any country, region or drawn area to see when fire seasons start and peak, whether a year was unusual, where it was unusual on the map, and how the latest week compares with the same week in earlier years, with phone alerts. Results agree with NASA MCD64A1 and GFED burned area (India seasonal r = 0.93) and predict held-out years (world annual total within a median of 1.6%). It is open, needs no login, and states its limits, helping responders, land managers and scientists anticipate critical fire periods.
details:
Global Burn Log turns 25 years of NASA satellite fire detections into a burning-activity calendar for any place on Earth. Pick a country, one of 16 featured regions, or draw or upload your own area. The app shows every day since 2000 as a calendar heatmap, the typical year and its normal range, the fire seasons of every year, whether the year was unusual, and a map of where it burned. A 60-second guided tour follows the Punjab and Haryana crop-residue burning story: when the season starts, when it peaks, and how the latest year compares (2025 was the quietest of the 25 years).

THE PROBLEM AND HOW WE SOLVED IT

Active-fire records come from different sensors that cannot be compared directly. VIIRS (375 m pixels) finds far more small fires than MODIS (1 km pixels), so a raw count for India jumps about 6.5 times in 2012 even though the country did not suddenly burn more. We:

1. Filter to vegetation fires at acceptable confidence.

2. Count "burning cell-days" on a hexagon grid (H3), which is far less sensitive to pixel size than raw fire counts.

3. Make VIIRS MODIS-equivalent: a VIIRS cell-day count only with two or more detections, since a lone small pixel is a fire MODIS would usually miss.

4. Learn seasonal ratios between MODIS Aqua and VIIRS (same overpass time) and between Terra and Aqua, and apply them to put 2000-2011 on one scale, with an uncertainty band on every estimated day.

5. Detect fire seasons, peaks and anomalies per area. After harmonising, the India jump falls from 6.5 times to 1.13 times.

CHECKING THAT IT IS RIGHT

We compared the result with independent NASA MCD64A1 burned area (India seasonal r = 0.93) and GFED burned area in 12 regions on six continents (average seasonal r = 0.84; seven regions at 0.90 or better). We also left each year out in turn and predicted it: the world's annual total was within a median of 1.6%. We tested alternatives and kept only what helped: the MODIS-equivalent rule cut held-out error from 5.3% to 3.9%, while per-biome calibration made results worse, so we rejected it.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

- Early-warning and emergency teams: a latest-week signal (newest near-real-time data against the same week in 2013-2025), a watchlist, and phone push alerts for the world and the featured regions, plus a countdown to a region's typical season start.

- Land managers: seasons for every year, whether the season is shifting, comparison with other regions, and a one-page report.

- Scientists: an open, reproducible cross-sensor record with its uncertainty, open data files, a notebook that opens in Colab, and the full pipeline on GitHub.

WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE

- It detects each fire season separately. A single "10% to 90% of activity" window spans February to November in Punjab and says nothing, because the region has two seasons.

- It draws an "Unusual" map that colours each cell against the same cell in 2013-2025, and a "Two years" map. Canada 2023 lights up where the record fires were.

- It reads the live feed with the same rule as the history and filters gas flares that would otherwise look like fires.

- It needs no server and no login. A custom area you draw is calibrated live in your browser using the same method as the Python pipeline, and the results matched exactly in our checks.

TOOLS

Python (pandas, PyArrow/Parquet, H3, NumPy) for the pipeline. React, Vite, MapLibre GL, deck.gl and D3 for the app. Firebase Hosting with a custom domain. A scheduled GitHub Action refreshes the latest-week signal daily. ntfy.sh delivers phone alerts. Data: NASA FIRMS (MODIS and VIIRS), NASA MCD64A1 through the Microsoft Planetary Computer, GFED4.1s, and optional Open-Meteo weather.

WHAT WE CONSIDERED

- No login, always-up access for judges and users, which led us to a static site.

- Honesty about uncertainty: estimated years are always labelled and drawn with a range.

- Accessibility and reach: works on phones, installable and usable offline, colour-blind safe colours, and an interface in English, Spanish, Portuguese and Hindi (the translations are AI-assisted and not yet reviewed by native speakers).

- Limits, stated on the site: cell-days show where and when fire was detected, not how much land burned; the match is weaker where a few huge fires dominate (Southeast Australia, Boreal Canada, California); NOAA-20 and NOAA-21 are not included; the near-real-time signal runs about 12 days behind. It is not for operational emergency decisions.

USE OF AI

Our team set the goal and made the design decisions. We used Claude (Anthropic) as a tool for planning and to help write the code and documentation. All fire data is real NASA data.
